query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled amount of Y and Hf as microalloying dopants via a laser cladding process will improve the performance of the uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy for fastener applications by enhancing thermal stability, corrosion resistance, and mechanical properties such as yield strength and creep resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with suboptimal strength and plasticity for industrial fastener applications.
generation.intervention: Y and Hf co-doping introduced through a laser cladding modification that forms a surface layer with the potential to precipitate an Al-rich L12 phase upon subsequent heat treatment.
generation.conditions: The alloy will be exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations (including high-temperature exposure up to ~900 °C), long-term mechanical loading (simulating service stresses), room-temperature creep conditions, and corrosive environments (e.g., molten salt environments such as 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl or chloride-containing acid solutions).
generation.structural_mediator: The intervention is expected to promote the formation of stable intermetallic precipitates (e.g., an Al-rich L12 phase) and improve grain boundary stability through segregation of Y and Hf, thereby modifying the microstructural evolution during heat treatment.
generation.mechanism: Y and Hf dopants are likely to segregate at grain boundaries and act as nucleation sites for the Al-rich L12 phase, which both refines the microstructure and improves the adhesion and stability of protective oxide scales. This should retard grain growth, reduce creep, and enhance resistance to hot corrosion by promoting a more stable, less spallation-prone oxide layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the Y and Hf co-doped alloy should exhibit improved high-temperature mechanical strength, reduced room-temperature creep rates, and enhanced corrosion resistance under both molten salt and acidic environments.
generation.baseline: The as-produced uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy without any dopant modification.
generation.boundary: The anticipated benefits are expected to hold under service conditions similar to those tested (up to ~900 °C in oxidizing and molten salt conditions, and under sustained mechanical loading and room-temperature creep). However, performance beyond these boundaries or under differing processing conditions may not achieve the same improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The exact improvement magnitude in strength, creep resistance, and corrosion performance is uncertain due to potential variations in dopant distribution and phase precipitation kinetics. Additionally, while evidence supports enhanced hot corrosion behavior with dopants, the combined effect on long-term mechanical properties remains to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set comprising the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and a second set with an identical matrix that has been modified via laser cladding with a controlled Y and Hf addition. Apply identical heat treatment schedules to both sets. Then, subject both sample groups to cyclic thermal fluctuations (including high-temperature exposures up to 900 °C), sustained mechanical loading to simulate long-term service, room-temperature creep tests, and corrosion exposure tests in chloride-containing molten salts and acid solutions.
measurements: Measurement of tensile and yield strengths, as well as creep rates, at relevant temperatures.
Quantification of corrosion resistance by measuring oxide scale spallation area and pitting density.
Microstructural characterization (phase analysis via X-ray diffraction; imaging via scanning electron microscopy) to assess precipitate formation and grain boundary features.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y and Hf co-doped samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements (e.g., >10% increase in high-temperature strength, reduction in creep rate, and demonstrably more stable and less spallation-prone oxide scales) relative to the baseline samples under the prescribed test conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. In this study, the Y and Hf co-doping did not change the microstructure morphology and phase structure of the coatings but did improve the thermal stability and resistance of the hot corrosion oxide scale spallation, providing a certain amount of data and theoretical support for the application of EHEA coat

## Abstract
In this work, the influence of temperature on the corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in a chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution was investigated using electrochemical measurement, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. Results show that the passive film of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is stable in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions at low temperatures, while an unstable film forms on the alloy at high temperatures. Furthermore, temperature changes the proportion of hydroxide and oxide in Fe and Cr, but it has no noticeable effect on Al and Ni, which is a significant factor on the passive behavior. L12 phase exhibits good corrosion resistance at different temperatures. Pitting occurred on B2 phase in the chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution at a low temperature of 5 °C, while pitting and dissolution take place on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 in the acid solution at room temperature and above.
